1:
How David enquired of the Lord here is a real difficulty, and the two who face it reach opposite solutions. Ellicott argues that the enquiry cannot have been made through the ephod, since the chapter itself says that Abiathar only joined David at Keilah, after the citizens had already asked for aid; so it was made through Gad the prophet, who was with David. He supports this from the parallel of Jehoshaphat enquiring of Micaiah, where the same formula is used. He then diagnoses the whole difficulty: the versions and the commentators failed to understand that enquiry of the Lord could be made in any other mode than through the Urim, and he holds that the Greek translators must have deliberately altered the Hebrew to escape it, rendering the verse so as to imply that Abiathar had come down with David to Keilah. Clarke takes the other road and does to the order of the text what Ellicott accuses the Greek of doing to its sense: the enquiry was probably by means of Abiathar, and therefore he thinks, with Houbigant, that the sixth verse should be read immediately after the first. Gill leaves the mechanism alone and gives the reasons for David's hesitation, that he had no commission from his prince and that his force was so small that attacking the Philistine army might be hazardous.

On why David went at all the commentary is unanimous and warm. Henry explains the prophet's earlier order as a commission: since Saul neglected the public safety, David was to take care of it notwithstanding the ill treatment given him, rendering good for evil and so being a type of him who not only ventured his life but laid it down for those who were his enemies. He also suggests a cause for the raid, that the departure of both God and David from Saul probably encouraged the Philistines, and draws the rule that the way for any country to be quiet is to let God's church be quiet in it. Henry admires the public spirit, that though his own hands were full and Saul sought his life he was willing to serve Saul's interests against the common enemy, and bravely abhorred the thought of sacrificing the common welfare to his private revenge; those are unlike David, Henry adds, who sullenly decline to do good because they have been ill used. Clarke makes the same point by naming the alternative: the adventure was truly noble, since had David not loved his country above private revenge he would have rejoiced in this invasion and in most cases a man with David's wrongs would have joined with his country's enemies.

Ellicott sets the episode in the decline of the reign it belongs to. Saul was becoming more and more neglectful of his higher duty of protecting his people, and as his malady increased his whole thoughts were concentrated on David's imaginary crimes, so that the history of the latter part of his reign is little more than a recital of his sad, bewildered efforts to compass the young hero's destruction. The task Saul abandoned, of protecting the people from constant Philistine marauding, was thereby entrusted to David, and pointing this out to him was evidently the first great mission of Gad the seer. On the men of Keilah's objection Ellicott clears up a geographical point, that saying they were afraid here in Judah does not imply Keilah lay outside the tribe's territory but only that the district round it was then under Philistine domination. Delitzsch gives the chapter its theological frame, that the events following show how the Lord on the one hand gave his servant pledges that he would eventually become king, and on the other plunged him into deeper and deeper trouble, to refine him and train him to be a king after his own heart.
7:
Gill observes that Saul must have been told why David went there, which one would have thought would have reconciled his mind to him; instead it only led him to contrive mischief. Henry presses past the ingratitude to the impiety: in saying God hath delivered him into my hand, Saul made providence patronise his malicious design, and he triumphed before the victory, forgetting how often he had held fairer advantages against David and missed his aim. One smiling providence, Henry warns, neither justifies an unrighteous cause nor secures its success. Ellicott finds the impiety in the vocabulary, the Hebrew word saying that God has repudiated or rejected him, where the Greek translators render it sold him. He also credits Saul with a calculation: there was little chance of taking a man roaming at large through the desert, but real hope of compassing his destruction by treachery or hand-to-hand encounter in a confined space like a city with bars and gates, and Saul knew too well what to expect of that faithless, thankless city. Henry adds that the summons abused the Israel of God as well, the people marched out under pretence of opposing the Philistines: miserable is that people whose prince is a tyrant, for some are sufferers by his tyranny and others are made instruments of it.

Ellicott notes that the earlier consultation is only said to have been made of the Lord, while here the narrative first records that Abiathar had arrived with the ephod and then has David direct him to bring it, pointedly connecting the enquiry with it; in that ephod were set twelve precious stones, one for each tribe, the tribal names engraved on them, and by ancient tradition only the high priest might use them as oracles. Clarke reads the scene more simply, as though David himself, clothed with the ephod, consulted the Lord. Wesley settles the manner of the answer: it came not by any change in the colour or situation of the stones but by a voice or suggestion from God to the high priest. Henry turns it to use. No sooner is the ephod brought than David employs it, and we who have the scriptures in our hands should take advice from them in doubtful cases and learn to say, Bring hither the Bible. He admires the prayer too, thrice calling himself God's servant, and solicitous less for himself than for the city: David does not say that Saul means to destroy me, but to destroy the city for my sake.

Both questions were answered, but not in the order asked. Gill takes it as a symptom, showing the perturbation of mind David was in. Ellicott reports Dean Payne Smith's view that the questions were put inversely to the logical order but according to their relative importance in David's mind, and cites the Talmud, that the enquirer is not to ask about two things at a time, since he will be answered about one only, and that the one he first uttered. Delitzsch draws the same rule from the text: the enquirer laid his matter before God in prayer and received an answer, but always to one question only, so David had to ask his first again. Clarke finds here an ample proof that there is such a thing as contingency in human affairs, God having poised many things between a possibility of being and not being; the answers carried conditions, that if David stayed Saul would come down and the men of Keilah would betray him, and because David left, neither happened. Wesley agrees that the answer, like the question, was upon supposition. So David went out with six hundred men, whithersoever they could go. Saul had said that God delivered David into his hand; Henry observes that God delivered him out of it, as a bird out of the snare of the fowler.
14:
Delitzsch fixes the ground: the desert of Judah is the tract between the mountains of Judah and the Dead Sea, and the desert of Ziph is the part surrounding that town, whose name survives in the ruins of Tell Zif. Ellicott puts the wilderness between Hebron and En-gedi while admitting that some stations in the future king's wanderings are only doubtfully identified; of the wood he notes that some read it as the proper name Horesh. Henry asks us first to commend David's conduct in these hiding places, his humility, fidelity to his prince and patient attendance on the providence of his God: he did not draw up his forces against Saul and avenge his own quarrel and that of the murdered priests, though that would have ended his troubles and the country's calamities, but kept God's way and waited God's time, content to secure himself in woods and wildernesses even though to some this might seem a reproach to the courage for which he had been famous. Then he asks us to lament the fate, that an innocent man should be put in fear of his life and a man of merit so recompensed.

That Saul sought him every day shows how restless his malice was, Henry adds, and that he sought his life, how cruel. Ellicott reads the same sentence as a general remark covering the remaining portion of Saul's reign, and hears in it a quiet irony: armed with all the power of the king in Israel, Saul was powerless, because the invisible King of Israel declined to give this hated David into his hand. Into that extremity comes Jonathan. Gill notes the twenty-two miles he travelled from Gibeah. Henry observes that David had likely appointed the time and place and that Jonathan kept the appointment though discovery might have cost him his life, true friendship shrinking neither from danger nor from condescension, but able to stoop and exchange a palace for a wood to serve a friend. Clarke insists that Jonathan could do all this consistently with his duty to his father and king. Ellicott rejects as untenable the idea that this interview was transposed here from the earlier secret meeting, since the narrative is circumstantial and names the scene.

Ellicott takes the phrase that Jonathan strengthened his hand in God as the narrator's signal of how sorely tried David was: the relentless hostility of his sovereign and once his friend, the apparent hopelessness of the struggle, the cruel ingratitude of whole bodies of his countrymen, and his homeless, outlawed condition all weighed on a temperament that was soon depressed, and his forebodings are breathed out in many of the Psalms. Henry and Wesley agree on the remedy. Jonathan was in no capacity to do anything for David, so he reminded him of the promise of God, the holy oil with which he had been anointed, and the singular providence with him hitherto, strengthening his hands for action by encouraging his heart not in the creature but in God. Henry calls him a self-denying friend as well, taking pleasure in David's advancement to an honour that was his own birthright and counting it preferment enough to be next him though under him; and since Saul knew this, he was wicked to persecute one whom God favoured and foolish to think he could disannul what God had purposed. Ellicott adds the pathos the record supplies: this friend found a grave on Mount Gilboa instead of a home with David, and had he lived he would surely have ceded his rights, unlike Ishbosheth, who set himself up as a rival claimant. Delitzsch notes that the covenant was a renewal by another solemn oath, after which Jonathan went home and David stayed in the wood; Wesley adds that they parted then and never met again in this world.
19:
Henry notes that David had put the more confidence in the people of that country because they were of his own tribe, and that they had reason to think themselves happy in serving the ornament of their tribe, a man so far from plundering their country that he was ready to protect it; yet to ingratiate themselves with Saul they told him exactly where David quartered and invited him down to take him, and they did it unasked, without even requesting a reward, as Judas did. Gill supplies a motive: terrified by what Saul had done to Nob, they judged it safest for their own security to inform against him. Ellicott reads their words and the king's reply as proof that they were warm adherents of Saul, entirely devoted to his fortunes and well aware of his desire to be rid of David. He also settles the geography: Jeshimon is not a place but a word for desert or solitude, used here of the dreary tract between the Dead Sea and the Hebron mountains, the wilderness of Judea the Gospel speaks of.

Henry hears the piety in Blessed be you of the Lord and remarks how near God was to his mouth though far from his heart; he hears self-pity in you have compassion on me, Saul looking on himself as an object of pity when it was his own envy and ill-nature that made him one, and insinuating meanwhile the little concern his other subjects showed him. Delitzsch traces it to an evil conscience: suspecting David of seeking to become his murderer, Saul thanked God in his delusion that the Ziphites had pity on him and had shown him the hiding place. When he adds that he hears David deals very subtilely, Henry answers that all David's subtlety was to secure himself, not to do mischief. Delitzsch sets out the charge: to reconnoitre the place where his foot came and find who had seen him there, lest false reports deceive him, then to come again with the certainty so that he might search David out among all the thousands of Judah; and Ellicott explains that the thousands were the greater tribal divisions, Judah being named as David's own tribe, where Saul probably found the larger number of his adherents. Henry thinks it strange Saul did not go down at once, and sees providence in a delay that gave David time to shift for himself.

Warned of the betrayal, David withdrew from Hachilah to the wilderness of Maon, which Delitzsch places less than four hours south of Hebron and two from Ziph; Ellicott finds the name preserved in a village on that hill. Henry assigns the fifty-fourth Psalm to this hour and draws the scene: Saul so close that there was but a mountain between, David and his men on one side flying and Saul and his men on the other pursuing, David in fear and Saul in hope, but the mountain an emblem of providence coming between David and the destroyer, like the pillar of cloud between Israel and the Egyptians. Clarke takes the messenger as providence exerted for David's life: God had already prepared the Philistine invasion and kept Saul ignorant how far David was in his power, the message arriving just at the point of time, before the scouts discovered him; Ellicott quotes a modern commentator calling it God's plan to save David, and Wesley adds that the wisdom of God is never at a loss for means to preserve his people. Henry suspects Saul would not have broken off the pursuit had no private interest of his own been at stake. On the name left behind, Delitzsch prefers the rock of smoothnesses, that is of slipping away or escaping, as better supported than the rock of divisions, which Clarke keeps with the Targum, the king's heart being divided to go hither and thither.
